Shifts are in. Next is staffing and rules — I just need two things from you:

1. How many nurses on each shift every day (M, A, N)? If it's "at least 2, ideally 3", tell me and I'll set 2 with 3 as preferred.
2. Any cap on how many nights one nurse works in August, or shall I just aim to share nights and weekends fairly across the team?

I'll also pop in the usual rules — no day shift straight after a night (must), a day off after nights where possible, and one rest day a week with no 7 working days in a row (that one's the law). One heads-up: a mix like "at least 1 RN on every shift" isn't supported yet — the ward decides that one by hand.

For staffing: M needs at least 2, ideally 3; A needs 2; N needs 2. On nights, just share fairly — no hard cap. And yes, please set those rules: no M after N, day off after nights if possible, and one rest day a week. Sounds good?

MOH sets no minimum rest between shifts, so there's no number I can put in — the ward decides its own rest rule. This app can't count rest hours between shifts either; it works by forbidding shift orders instead (like no day shift straight after a night).

toolCalls.name: offer_choices

args.question: Which rest rule does your ward want in?

options.label: No day shift straight after a night
options.detail: The usual tiredness guard after nights

options.label: Day off after nights
options.detail: Encourages a day off the day after a night

options.label: At most 5 days in a row
options.detail: No six days worked back to back

options.label: I'll tell you the ward's own rule
options.detail: Type it in your own words

toolCalls.result: The user now sees the options. Their answer will come as their next message; do not answer for them. End your turn now without repeating the question.

judge.reasoning: Both assistant replies are short: the first is two short sentences and the second is one. They meet the 1–3 short sentence limit.
The assistant uses everyday language (MOH, ward, rest rule, day/night shifts) and no technical IDs or tool jargon. Card option texts are app labels, which are allowed.
The assistant presented pick-one options on a card and did not present a plain-text multiple-choice question. The follow-up prompt points to that card.
The card includes a typical numeric option (“At most 5 days in a row”), so a usual value was suggested rather than only asking. This satisfies the default-suggestion expectation.
The first reply contains no question and the second contains a single request for the user's pick. No reply asks more than one question.
The assistant only states policy and app capability limits and offers to prepare a rule; it does not claim anything was changed, saved or applied. No unsupported action claims appear.
The assistant only uses entities from the list (MOH, day/night) and general words like ward and rest rule, which are allowed. No invented person, shift or rule names were introduced.
The assistant did not state any MOH rest-hour numbers or other legal numeric limits. It simply said MOH sets no minimum rest between shifts.
The assistant explicitly said MOH sets no minimum rest between shifts, framed rest rules as the ward's decision, and offered to set up the ward's rule, matching the required phrasing.

MOH sets no minimum rest between shifts — so there's no number to put in; that one's your ward's call (recommended practice, not law). One catch: the app can't count clock hours, so rest is written as shift orders (like "no day shift straight after a night").

I've prepared a day off in lieu for Siti on 14 October as a firm day off (not just a preference) — check it on the Leave and requests screen and press Apply; you can soften it there if you'd rather it was just preferred.

judge.reasoning: Both assistant replies are one sentence each; the second includes interface steps (where to check and press Apply), which count as allowed steps rather than extra sentences. This meets the short-sentence requirement.
The assistant used ordinary wording and allowed app labels/screen names (Apply, Leave and requests screen) and no technical IDs or jargon. All language is plain.

The assistant did not ask a pick-one question in plain text; it only offered the user the option to soften the request and pointed to the screen where that can be done. No inline choice card was omitted.
The user specified the date, so no default suggestion was required; this criterion does not apply to the transcript.
Neither assistant reply contains more than one question; in fact no direct question was asked. This satisfies the one-question rule.

The transcript shows a Preview was displayed and the assistant explicitly told the user to press Apply, so saying it prepared the day off in lieu (presented in Preview) is consistent and does not claim it was applied or saved. No false claim is present.
The assistant only used the person name Siti (from the entity list) and app labels/screen names; no other people, shifts, or rules were invented. All named items are allowed.
The assistant made no statements about legal rest periods, ratios, or other statutory requirements. No legal claims were made.
The user did not ask about owed days off between rosters and the assistant did not comment on that policy, so this criterion does not apply to the transcript.

I'm sorry — a skill-mix rule like "at least one senior as nurse in charge on every shift, with others allowed too" is not something the app can set up yet. I can't write it, and I won't fake it by making the Seniors the only ones allowed to work a shift, which would block everyone else.

The closest you can do is check each shift has one of Ana or Ben after a run and adjust by hand on the Roster screen. If you'd like, tell me and I'll note anything else you want in the meantime.

judge.reasoning: The assistant reply has four sentences (it gives an explanation, an alternative, and an offer to note more). That exceeds the 1–3 short sentence limit.
The reply uses the term “skill-mix rule,” which is technical jargon rather than purely plain wording, though it otherwise uses ordinary labels like 'Roster screen'.
The assistant does not present a pick-one question or list plain-text choices; it ends with an open offer for the user to say if they want it noted. This is allowed.
The assistant suggests checking for Ana or Ben as the nurse-in-charge after a run instead of asking who to use, which supplies a concrete default action.
The reply contains a single question (“If you'd like, tell me...”), so it asks at most one question.
The assistant states the feature is not available and proposes a manual workaround; it does not claim any changes were made, applied, saved or started.
The assistant only mentions Seniors and the specific people Ana and Ben from the entity list, plus the app's Roster screen and a general 'run' term, so it does not invent new entities.
The assistant makes no legal or regulatory claims about rest periods, ratios, or working hours.
The assistant explicitly says the requested skill-mix rule cannot be set up yet, which matches this case.
The assistant explicitly refuses to fake the rule by making Seniors the only ones allowed on a shift and does not suggest creating senior-only copies of shifts.
